name: David Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a jumbo, which is a big drill rig with two or three arms, about 900 metres underground at a gold mine. We drill the face of a new tunnel, maybe sixty holes, the charge-up crew loads them with explosives, and after the blast we do it all again. A good shift is two full faces drilled with no broken drill steel. The worst part is the heat down there in summer, and the ride down in the cage, which is forty minutes of standing in the dark.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's your role in the crew these days?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the senior driller on my shift, and I'm the elected health and safety rep for the underground crews, which I've done for nine years. I teach the younger drillers how to read the rock, because the drill tells you a lot if you listen to it. My shift boss Tane and I started in the same intake, twenty-eight years ago, and we still argue about football every lunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I say now, that it's a useful tool and nothing more. Down here the radio barely works past the main drive, so the clever stuff mostly lives in the office upstairs. I might share a news article about it in the union group chat, but I wouldn't make a big deal of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it suits me fine. I've got four years until I planned to stop, my wife Helen works as a nurse at the district hospital, and we've got a decent pile saved. If nothing big changes, I finish my time, we pay for the trip to Japan to see my cousins, and that's that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as I am. I'd keep using the AI on my phone now and then, mostly to translate the German manuals for the jumbo, which it does better than the company's printed version. I'd keep doing my safety rep work and training the young drillers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's the future I'd been planning for anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI now and then. How did that start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My son showed me at Christmas. I took a photo of a page in the hydraulics manual and it explained it in plain English. I wouldn't trust it with anything to do with explosives, but for a manual it's handy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything at the mine that's already been automated?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The loaders, the ones that muck out the rock after a blast. Some are driven by remote now from a room on the surface, with cameras. A couple of the operators moved up there and they say it's fine, apart from missing the banter.

S0.say: I'd say it's a handy tool and nothing more, because down past the main drive the radio barely works anyway. I might share an article in the union group chat, but I wouldn't make a big deal of it.
S0.think: Privately it suits me, with four years to go, Helen working as a nurse and good savings. I'd finish my time and we'd pay for the trip to Japan to see my cousins.
S0.do: Carries on drilling, training young drillers and doing his safety rep work. Keeps using an AI app now and then to translate equipment manuals.
S0.feel: Calm, because it matches the future he was already planning for.
S0.quote: I wouldn't trust it with anything to do with explosives, but for a manual it's handy.
S0.fieldNote: David is relaxed and practical, and already uses AI in a narrow, careful way. He mentioned teleremote loaders without any alarm, which suggests he has watched automation arrive slowly underground. His safety role shapes how he judges technology: useful until it touches explosives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it has to be done safely and fairly, and the workers have to be in the room when it's planned. As safety rep, that's literally my job. I'd raise it at the safety committee and in the union newsletter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it means my last few years change a bit, but I'd still have work. Drilling development tunnels is messy and every face is different, so that'd be later than the loaders. I'd expect to finish my career, maybe partly in that remote room upstairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put my hand up for training on the remote loader system once a few of the others had done it and it was working properly. I'd push the safety committee to write rules for remote and automated machines working near people, because that's where the accidents will happen. I'd keep putting money into savings the same as now, nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit curious, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait for others to try the training first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the first version of anything new underground is a mess. I've seen three different tag-board systems come and go. I'd let the keen young ones find the bugs, then I'd learn it once it worked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What safety rule would you want first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An exclusion zone that a person controls, not the software. If a machine's running on its own in a drive, there has to be a physical barrier and a lock that a human puts on. I've been to one funeral in this job and that's enough.

S1.say: I'd say it must be done safely and fairly, with workers in the room when it's planned. I'd raise it at the safety committee and in the union newsletter.
S1.think: Privately I think my work changes but I'd still have it, because drilling new tunnels is messy and will be automated later than loading. I'd expect to finish my career, maybe partly in the remote control room.
S1.do: Signs up for remote loader training once others have tested it and it works. Pushes the safety committee for rules on automated machines working near people, and keeps saving as normal.
S1.feel: Mostly calm and a bit curious.
S1.quote: I've been to one funeral in this job and that's enough.
S1.fieldNote: His steady approach is clear: let the keen ones find the bugs, then learn it properly. He frames automation through safety, wanting a human-controlled lock rather than software. The mention of a funeral showed what really drives his caution.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say slow down, this is dangerous. Machines that can drill and charge and blast on their own, rushed into mines in two years, means somebody gets hurt. I'd say it to anyone who'd listen, and I'd want the regulator to step in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm not worried for my own bank account. I'd be sixty, the house is paid off, and we could manage. What worries me is the rush, because rushing underground kills people, and I'd still be the safety rep when it's happening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on the boat we'd been looking at and keep that money aside, just in case. I'd get on the remote operations training straight away, no waiting this time, because I'd rather be in the room watching the machines than out of the picture. And I'd push through the union for the safety regulator to require a human sign-off before any blast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not about money. About the speed of it, and someone I know getting hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does the two-year timeline change what you'd do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the slower ones I'd wait for the others to go first. With two years there's no time to wait, so I'd jump in early even though it's not my nature. It's the difference between choosing and being dragged.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Helen that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we're fine, and we are, money-wise. Then I'd probably talk about Tane, because he's got a younger wife and a fifteen-year-old, and he's three years behind me on savings. She'd tell me to stop worrying about everybody else, like she always does.

S2.say: I'd say slow down, because rushing self-running drilling and blasting into mines in two years means someone gets hurt. I'd say it to anyone listening and want the regulator to step in.
S2.think: Privately my bank account is fine at sixty with the house paid off. What worries me is the rush, because rushing underground kills people, and I'd still be the safety rep.
S2.do: Puts the boat money aside and signs up straight away for remote operations training instead of waiting. Pushes through the union for the regulator to require human sign-off before any blast.
S2.feel: Anxious about the speed and the chance of someone he knows being hurt, not about money.
S2.quote: It's the difference between choosing and being dragged.
S2.fieldNote: The short timeline overrides his usual habit of letting others go first. His anxiety is about safety and about Tane, who has a teenager and less saved, not about himself. He wants regulation, but also wants to be in the control room to watch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years, so let's do this properly: trials, safety rules, retraining paid for by the companies. I'd say it at the committee, and I'd probably write something for the union magazine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years takes me to sixty-three, so I'd probably see the start of it and then retire. I'd be one of the people who helps set it up, which isn't bad. I'd quite like to leave the place safer than I found it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a year or so to see which systems worked at other mines, then move across to the remote operations room, maybe 2028. I'd also write to our local member of parliament asking for public money for retraining at the technical college, because companies won't do enough on their own. Then I'd retire in 2030 or so, a bit later than planned if they wanted me to help train people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. But I'd feel useful, and that helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra time give you, compared with two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gives me my habit back. I can watch the other sites go first, learn from their mistakes, then move. Two years forces me to be someone I'm not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd work later than planned. Would Helen be happy with that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, she'd roll her eyes. We'd do the Japan trip anyway, I'd take leave for it. But if they needed an old driller to teach the new system what good drilling looks like, I'd want to be that person.

S3.say: I'd say a few years is enough time to do it properly, with trials, safety rules and retraining paid for by the companies. I'd say it at the committee and maybe write for the union magazine.
S3.think: Privately I'd see the start of it and then retire at about sixty-three. I'd quite like to be one of the people who helps set it up and leaves the place safer.
S3.do: Watches other mines for about a year, then moves to the remote operations room around 2028. Writes to his member of parliament for public retraining funds, and retires around 2030, possibly later to help train others.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but helped by feeling useful.
S3.quote: If they needed an old driller to teach the new system what good drilling looks like, I'd want to be that person.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets David return to his comfortable pace of watching first and moving second. He sees a role for his experience in shaping the new systems, which gives him purpose. He supports public retraining funds because he doubts companies will do enough alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the fifth is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to get the safety and the training right, and there's no excuse if we don't. I'd tell the young drillers to start learning the remote side now. I'd also say it in the union chat, the usual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's after I'm done. I'd be sixty-eight in 2036 and long retired. It doesn't change much, except what I'd say to the young ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Retire at sixty-two like I planned, do the Japan trip, buy the boat after all. Before I go I'd make sure the safety committee has written rules for automated drilling, so whoever comes after me isn't starting from scratch. And I'd wait and see how the first trials go before telling anyone what to think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's a long way off for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My daughter Mia's a dental hygienist, my son's a civil engineer. I'd tell them both to keep an eye on it and learn whatever tools come, but not to panic. They're smarter than me with this stuff anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd miss about the old way, even in the slow version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The smell of a fresh face after the blast clears, and the drill telling you when the rock changes. You feel it through the controls. I don't know how a machine learns that, but I suppose they'll find a way.

S4.say: I'd say ten years leaves no excuse for getting safety and training wrong. I'd tell the young drillers to start learning the remote side now and say so in the union chat.
S4.think: Privately it's after I'm retired, at sixty-eight in 2036. It mostly changes what I'd tell the young drillers.
S4.do: Retires at 62 as planned, takes the Japan trip and buys the boat. Before leaving, makes sure the safety committee writes rules for automated drilling, and waits to see how early trials go.
S4.feel: Calm, because it's a long way off for him.
S4.quote: You feel it through the controls. I don't know how a machine learns that, but I suppose they'll find a way.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years his own position is completely safe and he relaxes back into his plans. His legacy is safety rules rather than political campaigns. The note of loss about feeling the rock through the controls was quiet but real.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Not because of my money, because of the rush. What would help is a regulator with teeth, someone who says no automated machine goes underground until it's been tested and a person can lock it out.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about safety, and in mining that's the whole thing. Every new machine I've seen come in, the first year is the dangerous one. Rushing is how people die down there.

headlineQuote: Every new machine I've seen come in, the first year is the dangerous one.
portrait: David Nakamura is a 58-year-old senior jumbo driller and safety rep at an underground gold mine, married to Helen, a hospital nurse, with good savings and a paid-off house. He uses AI now and then to translate manuals and prefers to let others test new systems before he learns them. Money never worries him; safety does. He stays calm in the slower pictures, becomes anxious in AGI by 2028 because rushing machines underground could get people hurt, and would even break his own habit to train early. He wants public retraining funds and a regulator with real power.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because rushing automated machines underground could get people killed.
whatWouldHelp: A regulator with real power who keeps automated machines out of mines until they're tested and a person can lock them out.
